title: Estuarine Biofilm Communities Adapt to Changing Conditions While Retaining Crucial Pollutant‐Combatting Functions
content:
Intertidal microphytobenthic biofilms were collected from the sediment–water interface of an Indian estuarine mangrove forest. Field samples and biofilms cultured under controlled conditions showed site‐specific microbial succession and ecological roles. Culture conditions reshaped community structure, though microbial diversity and core functional profiles were broadly preserved.

ABSTRACT
Industrialization has increased the influx of toxicants into intertidal and estuarine ecosystems. Intertidal sediments are exposed to heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pesticides, and other xenobiotics through effluents, shipping, spillages, battery disposal, and agricultural run‐off. Pollutants accumulate in sediments, disrupting nutrient cycling and impairing primary productivity, thereby threatening coastal food webs. Sediment‐bound biofilms or microphytobenthos are complex assemblages of microorganisms embedded in extracellular polymeric substances and play vital roles in biogeochemical cycling, sediment stabilization, and pollutant remediation. Their functional responses to contaminant exposure remain poorly understood, particularly in tropical estuaries. Biofilms from contaminated estuarine sediments were analysed using metagenome‐assembled genomes (MAGs) and genome‐scale metabolic models (GEMs) in a paired field‐laboratory approach. Greater metabolic diversity of field biofilms indicated broader functional capacities to sustain pollutant exposure. Conserved genes linked to organic compound degradation and metal transport co‐occurred across MAGs, suggesting integrated detoxification strategies. GEM‐based simulations revealed metabolic cross‐feeding underlying contaminant transformation. Culture conditions shaped microbial succession and ecological roles, yet core pollutant degradation and nutrient processing functions persisted, operated by dominant taxa. Microphytobenthic experimental studies rely on laboratory‐cultured communities derived from field‐collected samples. Contrasting community dynamics and altered metabolism due to ‘bottle effect’ are foundational for correctly interpreting laboratory‐based experimental outcomes.

title: Insight Into the Evolution of Symbiosis in the Cupriavidus Genus: Highly Conserved Symbiotic Island and a Patchy Phylogenetic Distribution
content:
Symbiotic Cupriavidus bacteria comprise five distinct evolutionary lineages. While their core nodulation and nitrogen‐fixing genes share a highly conserved ancestral origin, the plasmids carrying them display a highly variable mosaic structure, revealing a complex evolutionary history for legume symbiosis in beta‐rhizobia.

ABSTRACT
Currently, diversity and evolutionary studies on beta‐rhizobia have primarily focused on Paraburkholderia, leaving the evolutionary history of symbiosis in the Cupriavidus genus largely unexplored. The present work provides an updated view of symbiotic Cupriavidus diversity and analyses the origin and evolution of their nitrogen‐fixing capabilities. Using whole‐genome phylogenetic reconstructions, we demonstrate that symbiotic Cupriavidus strains belong to five distinct evolutionary lineages, intermixed with non‐symbiotic species. Comparative genomics revealed high synteny and sequence conservation within the symbiotic island across all lineages, suggesting a single ancestral acquisition of the nod‐nif‐fix clusters. However, in contrast, we observed very low sequence conservation among the (mega)plasmids carrying these genes. This finding definitively excludes the existence of a universal conserved replicon carrying the symbiotic genes within beta‐rhizobia. Instead, our results reveal a mosaic evolutionary pattern where a highly conserved symbiotic island is mobilized across highly variable plasmid backbones. Ultimately, our findings highlight that the distribution of symbiotic traits in Cupriavidus has been shaped by a complex interplay of horizontal gene transfer, plasmid remodelling, and host‐driven selective pressures, positioning South America as a key hotspot for beta‐rhizobial biodiversity.

title: Tree height uncertainty biases aboveground biomass estimation more than wood density in miombo woodlands
content:
Tree height uncertainty biases aboveground biomass estimation more than wood density in miombo woodlands
Arthur M. Yambayamba, Ferdinand Handavu, Kondwani Kapinga, and Tommaso Jucker
Biogeosciences, 23, 7955–7972, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7955-2026, 2026
Trees contribute enormously to climate change mitigation by sequestering huge amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide. Quantifying this important function of trees is however not without challenges as it requires measuring the size and density of trees to determine aboveground biomass. Our study shows that uncertainty in tree size can lead to more errors than from density. Characterising local tree structures is key to our understanding of the contribution of trees to climate change mitigation.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics and drivers of bare soil albedo in European croplands
content:
Spatiotemporal dynamics and drivers of bare soil albedo in European croplands
Ke Yu, Yang Su, Philippe Ciais, Ronny Lauerwald, David Makowski, Tianqi Shi, Shengbiao Wu, Petra Sieber, Chuanlong Zhou, and Daniel S. Goll
Biogeosciences, 23, 7973–7991, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7973-2026, 2026
Bare soil reflectance affects surface energy exchange in agricultural systems, but its field-scale variability is still poorly known. Using satellite observations and machine learning, we examined spatiotemporal variations of bare soil reflectance across European croplands. We show that it varies with soil properties, soil moisture, and observation geometry. These results suggest that dynamic soil reflectance should be taken into account in surface energy balance studies of agroecosystems.

title: Fate of legacy ammonium in the coastal Baltic Sea
content:
Fate of legacy ammonium in the coastal Baltic Sea
Dana Hellemann, Xiaole Sun, Tom Jilbert, Eva Ehrnsten, Bo Gustafsson, Lora Harris, Christoph Humborg, Bärbel Müller-Karulis, and Alf Norkko
Biogeosciences, 23, 7993–8015, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7993-2026, 2026
Using model-simulations and field data, we assess the effect of past eutrophication on present and future ammonium dynamics in coastal sediments of the Baltic Sea. Our results indicate a persistent but mild eutrophication legacy effect on sediment-water ammonium release, which is stronger driven by external organic matter loading. The results highlight that external organic matter loading needs to be reduced to also reduce ammonium loading to the coastal ecosystem and enable ecosystem recovery.

title: What Sets the AMOC's Sensitivity to CO2 Forcing? The Role of Background Mean‐State and Density Balance
content:
Abstract
The future evolution of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) under anthropogenic forcing remains highly uncertain, partly because the role of the background ocean state in conditioning AMOC sensitivity is not fully understood. Using CMIP6 simulations under abrupt‐4 × CO2 and SSP‐585 forcing, we investigate how mean‐state thermal and haline density compensation in the western subpolar North Atlantic influences AMOC decline. Models are classified into thermallydominated, salinity‐dominated, and balanced‐compensation regimes based on their subsurface density structure in the western subpolar North Atlantic. Models farther from balanced thermal–haline compensation experience substantially larger AMOC weakening, associated with enhanced upper‐ocean stratification and reduced deep convection. Salinity‐dominated models tend to have the strongest initial AMOC and weakest stratification in the western subpolar North Atlantic, but have the largest absolute and percentage forced AMOC decline. Balanced‐compensation models retain persistent convection in the Nordic Seas and exhibit the smallest AMOC decline, whereas salinity‐dominated models undergo rapid stratification‐driven weakening linked to surface freshening and convection collapse. Thermally‐dominated models have the weakest initial AMOC state and weaken more gradually due to residual haline compensation at depth, but still represent a large percentage AMOC decline. While background AMOC strength explains much of the inter‐model spread in absolute AMOC decline, including thermal and haline density compensation consistently improves the explanation of inter‐model differences across both forcing scenarios. Together, these results demonstrate that AMOC sensitivity depends not only on its initial strength, but also on the underlying thermohaline structure of the subpolar North Atlantic.

title: Sensitivity of Biogeochemical Simulations to Time‐Varying Light Attenuation and Its Uncertainties in the Red Sea
content:
Abstract
The light attenuation coefficient Kd ${K}_{d}$ controls underwater light availability and strongly influences marine biogeochemical dynamics. Despite its importance, most ocean biogeochemical models prescribe static climatologies of Kd ${K}_{d}$, neglecting its spatiotemporal variability and observational uncertainty. The consequences of these simplifications for simulated marine ecosystems remain poorly understood. Here we investigate the sensitivity of marine biogeochemical simulations to space and time‐varying Kd ${K}_{d}$ and its associated uncertainties in the Red Sea. We construct an ensemble of monthly Kd ${K}_{d}$ spatial fields from a multi‐sensor merged satellite product providing both attenuation estimates and uncertainty information. The data set reveals pronounced spatiotemporal variability, with higher turbidity and larger uncertainties in the southern basin and clearer conditions in the north. To quantify the impact of time‐varying Kd ${K}_{d}$, we design controlled experiments using the Massachusetts Institute of Technology General Circulation Model‐nitrogen‐version of Biogeochemistry with Light, Iron, Nutrients, and Gases (NBLING) system, where physical circulation and driving fields are constrained by data assimilation within an ensemble framework. The spatio‐temporally varying Kd ${K}_{d}$ ensemble is prescribed as input to the NBLING ecosystem model, enabling a controlled comparison between simulations driven by time‐mean and time‐varying spatial maps of Kd ${K}_{d}$. The results show pronounced subsurface responses, particularly near the lower euphotic boundary. Time‐varying Kd ${K}_{d}$ intensifies summer deep chlorophyll maximum peaks by 10%–20% and reveals contrasting ecosystem states during the 2015 El Nińo. Comparisons with satellite and in situ observations indicate improved representation of vertical ecosystem structure. Sampling the Kd ${K}_{d}$ ensemble increases the spread of simulated biogeochemical fields by up to 100% within the euphotic layer, reflecting model sensitivity to optical variability and highlighting the importance of representing it in ocean biogeochemical models.

title: Chlorophyll Response to Freshwater and Wind Forcing in a Coastal Ecosystem: Recent Decades and Future Climate Scenarios
content:
Abstract
Climate change is reshaping coastal ecosystems by altering freshwater inputs, salinity, and stratification, which contribute to regulating nutrient dynamics, primary productivity, and carbon cycling. This study examines surface chlorophyll variability in the Gulf of Naples (Mediterranean Sea) using long‐term monitoring data, reanalysis products, and machine learning to identify the roles of freshwater input, surface salinity, stratification, and wind in regulating phytoplankton biomass accumulation. The emergence of salinity as a primary predictor of chlorophyll concentration confirms the role of freshwater inflows and stratification as key modulators of primary productivity, acting through combined physical and biogeochemical pathways. To exploit this predictive potential without relying on in situ data, we develop an empirical model to link salinity to its main drivers. Surface salinity is estimated from freshwater proxies and mixed‐layer depth, demonstrating that the predictive skill of the model remains robust even when using indirect predictors. Further, we establish a cascade approach to predict chlorophyll responses from wind and freshwater proxies, using a Random Forest framework. Building on this framework, we use climate projections (RCP4.5, RCP8.5) up to 2070 to explore potential changes in primary production. Our model suggests a progressive increase in salinity and a decline in chlorophyll, particularly in spring. As expected, land‐based changes (e.g., precipitation, basin catchment effects) exert a strong influence on coastal ecosystems. These findings point to the importance of long‐term monitoring and interdisciplinary approaches to enhance understanding of the functioning of ecosystems to better manage them under future climate scenarios.

title: Synoptic Pathways of Mid‐Depth Salinity Maximum Intrusions in the South Brazil Bight
content:
Abstract
Cross‐shelf exchanges play a crucial role in distributing heat, salt, and biogeochemical properties between the continental shelf and the open ocean. Among the processes shaping these exchanges, the intrusion of warm and salty waters (mid‐depth Salinity Maximum, Smax ${S}_{\max }$) remains poorly understood in the South Brazil Bight (SBB). We present observational evidence of Smax ${S}_{\max }$ intrusions in the Northeastern SBB (NE‐SBB) based on hydrographic observations collected between February and March 2022. Using a multi‐platform observational data set combined with Lagrangian particle tracking, we show that Smax ${S}_{\max }$ originate north of the study region and were advected southward primarily by the Brazil Current (BC). Two dominant advective pathways are identified: (a) a southwestward along‐shelf route associated with a non‐meandering BC, and (b) a cross‐shelf pathway driven by the interaction between the BC meander and the cyclonic Cabo Frio Eddy that is intensified by the presence of an eddy dipole. Once Smax ${S}_{\max }$ reaches the shelf break, its penetration onto the continental shelf is wind‐driven, mid‐depth onshore counterflow during upwelling‐favorable conditions, as suggested by the Burger number analysis higher than 1. These results highlight a two‐step mechanism for Smax ${S}_{\max }$ intrusions in the NE‐SBB, where mesoscale dynamics govern remote delivery to the shelf edge, while wind‐driven circulation and stratification regulate onshore penetration and vertical structure. By elucidating the pathways and mechanisms of Smax ${S}_{\max }$ intrusions, this study advances the understanding of cross‐shelf exchanges in the SBB and emphasize the importance of remotely forced processes in shaping the thermodynamics and biogeochemistry of subtropical continental shelves.

title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
content: Sensory neurons are traditionally viewed as feature detectors that respond with an increase in firing rate to preferred stimuli while remaining unresponsive to others. Here, we identify a dual-feature encoding strategy in macaque visual cortex, wherein many neurons in areas V1 and V4 are selectively tuned to two distinct visual features—one that enhances and one that suppresses activity—around an elevated baseline firing rate. By combining neuronal recordings with functional digital twin models—deep learning-based predictive models of biological neurons—we were able to systematically identify each neuron’s preferred and non-preferred features. These feature pairs served as anchors for a continuous, low-dimensional axis in natural image similarity space, along which neuronal activity varied approximately linearly. Within a single visual area, visual features that strongly or weakly activated individual neurons also had a high probability of modulating the activity of other neurons, suggesting a shared feature selectivity across the population that structures stimulus encoding. We show that this encoding strategy is conserved across species, present in both primary and lateral visual areas of mouse cortex. Dual-feature selectivity is consistent with recent anatomical evidence for feature-specific inhibitory connectivity, complementing the feature-detector principle through circuit mechanisms in which selective excitation and inhibition may together enhance the representational capacity of the neuronal population.

title: Urban Building Foundations Alter Seawater Intrusion Dynamics in Coastal Aquifers
content:
Abstract
Coastal aquifers are threatened by seawater intrusion (SWI) from sea‐level rise (SLR) and storm surges. Vulnerability is highest in urban areas, where dense populations rely on fresh groundwater and saltwater can damage subsurface infrastructure. The effects of deep building foundations on transient SWI and recovery remain insufficiently understood. Three‐dimensional variable‐density simulations show that, at quasi‐steady state, low‐permeability foundations displace the interface slightly landward by reducing the effective flow cross‐section. Under SLR, foundations slow intrusion once saltwater reaches the foundation zone. Under storm surges, buildings with full‐depth foundations in the low‐permeability aquifer reduce peak whole‐aquifer excess salt mass by 38.8% and prolong its 90% flushing time by 41 years relative to the case without foundations. Aquifer permeability controls foundation‐zone salinization timing and post‐surge recovery rates. By stalling saltwater and impeding flushing, foundations may accelerate their corrosion, even without groundwater pumping. As coastal cities expand, the presence of foundations may exacerbate stresses on urban freshwater resources and infrastructure.

title: Monitoring Wind Turbine Vibrations for Structural and Subsurface Insights
content:
Abstract
Wind turbines generate continuous seismic signals that encode information about their structural integrity and surrounding environment. Utilizing 16 months of passive seismic data from two wind farms in Illinois, we analyze these turbine vibrations to evaluate both structural dynamics and near‐surface hydrogeology. We detected a precursory spectral anomaly 2 days before a turbine collapse, indicating initial structural tilting before visual signs emerged. Beyond structural health, temporal variations in turbine vibration frequencies serve as an empirical proxy for the critical zone's poroelastic state. By leveraging these frequency shifts, our model reconstructs first‐order spatial soil‐moisture patterns consistent with lithologic contrasts inferred from airborne electromagnetic data. Because this retrospective proof‐of‐concept relies on a single collapse event and noncollocated hydrological data, independent deployments with collocated sensors are required to assess generalizability. Nevertheless, these initial findings suggest wind energy infrastructure provides a promising dual‐purpose framework for structural monitoring and spatio‐temporal tracking of near‐surface hydrological processes.

title: Interstitial Aerosol Water Uptake Limits Fog Supersaturation
content:
Abstract
Fogs over polluted regions often exhibit extremely low supersaturation, yet the controlling mechanisms remain poorly constrained. Existing frameworks attribute supersaturation adjustment mainly to competition among activated droplets, while the role of interstitial aerosol water has been largely overlooked due to observational limitations. Here, we develop a new approach based on an advanced optical instrument to achieve online, size‐resolved quantification of interstitial aerosol water uptake. By combining optical measurements with a machine learning–constrained framework, we retrieve dry aerosol volume and hygroscopic growth at saturation of interstitial aerosols, enabling fog water budget analysis. Observations on the North China Plain show that interstitial aerosol water contributes >50% of total fog water during formation and remains comparable (>25%) to droplet water throughout evolution. This competition helps suppress the supersaturation to <0.03%, limiting aerosol activation and droplet growth. These results identify interstitial aerosol water as a key regulator of fog supersaturation in polluted atmospheres.

title: Inferring changes in pico- and nanophytoplankton assemblages from long-term coastal thermohaline observations
content:
Inferring changes in pico- and nanophytoplankton assemblages from long-term coastal thermohaline observations
Mathilde Couteyen Carpaye, David Nerini, David Pecqueur, Léa Buniak, Morgane Didry, Jean-Marc Feuerstein, Fabrice Garcia, Véronique Lagadec, Sandra Nunige, Christophe Salmeron, and Gérald Grégori
Ocean Sci., 22, 3657–3692, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3657-2026, 2026
Monitoring of phytoplankton over long periods and at high frequency is challenging. Yet, it is essential because these organisms form the base of marine food webs, and changes in their communities can affect higher trophic levels. Here, we address the challenge of missing biological data by using vertical profiles of temperature and salinity as proxies for environmental conditions influencing nutrient availability and shaping pico- and nanophytoplankton communities at a coastal site.

title: Low-fidelity simulator selection for multi-fidelity inference of epithelial vertex models
content: Vertex models link cell division, neighbour exchange, and intercellular forces to epithelial tissue form through parameters such as junctional line tension and perimeter contractility. Bayesian inference of these parameters from data quantifies their uncertainty, but for stochastic models of proliferating tissues it requires many costly simulations. Multi-fidelity simulation-based inference reduces this cost by training on many runs of a cheaper, less accurate ('low-fidelity') simulator before refining with a few full ('high-fidelity') runs. Low-fidelity versions can be constructed in several ways, for example by stopping simulations early, coarsening the timestep, or averaging fewer replicates, but it is unclear which to choose before committing to costly training. To address this, we introduce PRISM (Paired Ranking Index for Simulator Matching), a screen that compares each candidate with the full simulator on paired runs, scoring  agreement in cell-packing statistics against cost. For a vertex model of a proliferating tissue, PRISM flags stopping early as unreliable before training; once trained, this choice can produce confidently wrong parameter estimates. By contrast, a coarser timestep, within the range tested, is cheap and accurate; while fewer replicates are accurate but too costly. Using a screened low-fidelity simulator, multi-fidelity inference outperforms approximate Bayesian computation and neural-network inference trained on full simulations alone, at matched cost and with well-calibrated uncertainty. The same pattern recurs for a second vertex model fitted to published Drosophila pupal-wing imaging data, although there stopping halfway proves safe. Together, our findings suggest that which approximations are safe depends on the model, and that screening them before training makes multi-fidelity inference of tissue mechanics practical.

title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
content: Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish (Danio rerio), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model's floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30-43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful.

title: Choice of annotation data significantly impacts automated reconstruction of genome-scale metabolic networks
content: Genome-scale metabolic models are valuable tools for studying metabolism in many applications, such as metabolic engineering or understanding human disease. However, curated models are available for only a limited number of organisms, and generating high-quality models for additional organisms remains a challenge. To help address this challenge, several software tools have been developed that can produce draft models in an automated fashion, but the quality of these draft models lags behind manually curated ones. Thus, there is still a need to improve these tools. Previous work has focused primarily on developing better methods for each step in the reconstruction process, such as gene annotation and gap-filling. Here, we focus on the data that underlies these methods, such as known connections between protein sequence and function. We find that changing the source of reconstruction data has a substantial impact on the contents and predictions of generated models. In fact, the source of data can have a bigger impact than the choice of reconstruction method. Additionally, we show that the reconstruction process is sensitive to the accuracy of gene annotations in the reconstruction data. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of having functional annotation data from an organism that is closely related to the one for which a model is being built. These observations highlight the importance of reconstruction data and identify principles that should be considered when selecting data for reconstruction tools.

title: Cell cycling throttles epithelial--mesenchymal transition
content: Cell cycle phase is an understudied source of variation in gene expression. EMT is a case in point: this cell state transition that drives metastasis has been studied widely across tissue, stimulus, and microenvironmental conditions, yet cell cycle effects are routinely regressed out of single-cell EMT analyses. Here, we compare EMT between G1 and cycling (S/G2/M) cell states in two independent scRNA-seq datasets of TGF-{beta}-stimulated MCF10A mammary epithelial cells (varying dose and timepoint). G1 cells consistently show higher expression of EMT genes and upregulated RNA velocities than cycling cells, with the strongest upregulation in G1 EMT intermediate states. Consistent with the go-or-grow hypothesis, EMT and cell cycle programs inversely correlate; moreover, this anticorrelation extends to RNA velocity and strengthens with TGF-{beta} dose. We identify a 77-gene G1-specific EMT signature enriched for actin cytoskeletal and extracellular matrix genes that would otherwise be lost by regressing out cell cycle effects. This gene set prompts the hypothesis that, unconstrained by the cytoskeletal demands of mitosis, G1 cells have greater capacity to execute EMT. Further, we developed an EMT gene regulatory model coupled with a cell cycle module, and found through simulation that the model recapitulated this inverse EMT--cell cycle relationship. Using this model, we predict that cycle-selective chemotherapy enriches for the G1 intermediate state, which has high metastatic potential. Cell cycle phase thus ought not be regressed out of EMT states, given its influence on EMT.

title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the pigtail macaque lung
content: Background: The lungs undergo substantial physiological and immunological changes during respiratory illness to meet the host's increased metabolic and oxygen demands. These responses require coordination among epithelial, endothelial, stromal, and immune cells throughout the respiratory zone, interstitium, and vasculature. Nonhuman primates (NHPs) are a valuable model for studying pulmonary biology as they have similar anatomic, physiologic, and immunologic correspondence to humans. Despite the widespread use of NHPs in pulmonary research, the cellular diversity and molecular characteristics of the pigtail macaque lung remain incompletely defined. Methods: Parenchymal lung tissue from five adult female pigtail macaques (Macaca nemestrina) was dissociated into single cells and profiled using 10x Genomics 3' single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq). Next, ambient RNA was removed and quality control analyses performed. Samples were then integrated using scVI and scANVI. Cell types were labeled after unsupervised clustering and subclustering, followed by manual annotation using canonical marker genes. We compared lineages and cell types with the Level 4 Human Lung Cell Atlas (HLCA) using scArches reference mapping and with the Rhesus Immune Reference Atlas (RIRA) using Seurat label transfer. Results: The atlas includes 61,323 cells representing 37 cell types in epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, lymphoid, and myeloid populations. Annotated populations included both major and rare lung cell types, including alveolar type I and II cells, club and multiciliated cells, aerocyte capillary, and lymphatic endothelial cells, pre-terminal bronchiole secretory cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and several innate-like lymphocyte populations (gamma delta T cells, MAIT-like cells, innate-like CD8+ T cells, and group 3 innate lymphoid cells). There was strong concordance at HLCA annotation level 4, including AT1 and AT2 cells (96% and 93%), B cells (94 to 97%), CD4+ T cells (99 to 100%), classical and non-classical monocytes (84% and 85%), alveolar macrophages (80%), and mast cells (96%). Immune populations mapped to the RIRA with similar fidelity (alveolar macrophages and B cells, 99%). Conclusions: While studies of pandemic respiratory infections, vaccines, and therapeutics rely on NHP disease models, this atlas provides a unique reference for epithelial, endothelial, stromal, and immune cell states in the pigtail macaque lung. We found that single-cell populations from the pigtail macaque lung are highly similar to those in the human lung at the lineage level. This reference will enable studies of pathogenesis and vaccine and drug efficacy in a highly translational model of the human lung.

title: Multi-Enzyme Data-Independent Acquisition Mass Spectrometry for Proteoform-Aware Single-shot Proteomics
content: Biological regulation does not operate at the level of the protein but across ensembles of protein variants shaped by alternative splicing, post-translational modification and endogenous proteolytic processing. Yet most conventional bottom-up discovery proteomics workflows remain optimized for a canonical protein census, leaving much of the sequence-level variation invisible. Multi-enzyme digestion has been recognized as an effective strategy to expand sequence coverage and proteoform sensitivity, but existing implementations rely on resource-heavy per-enzyme liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis, dedicated measurements for spectral library construction, and semi-manual reconciliation across multiple software tools, restricting the use to specialized laboratories and limited sample cohorts. Here we introduce mE-DIA, a multi-enzyme, proteoform-resolved data independent acquisition (DIA)-MS workflow that multiplexes complementary protease digested samples into a single DIA injection and processes them through a library-free pipeline within a single analysis engine, without supplemental data dependent acquisition (DDA)-MS measurements. The mE-DIA Pipeline graphical user interface orchestrates the analysis, and a dedicated proteoform inference algorithm and the interactive mE-DIA Peptide Mapper viewer make the sequence-level evidence explorable. Comparing the workflow to prevailing DDA-library-based multi-enzyme DIA on the same raw data and within shared search space showed increased identified protein groups by 30 % and protein groups quantified at [≤] 20 % CV by 47 %. A three-enzyme multiplex of the human pathogen Streptococcus pyogenes resolved 990 protein-backbone variants among 309 canonical protein entries, 1.8-fold more than the most productive single-enzyme analysis, including an H69 C-terminal proteoform of the ribosomal protein uS19 that the trypsin-only workflow did not resolve. By consolidating multi-enzyme acquisition, analysis and proteoform interpretation into one accessible toolset, mE-DIA brings sub-gene-resolved evidence within reach of routine single-shot discovery DIA proteomics.

title: Reversible decrease in swimming motility accompanies emergent β-lactam antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli
content: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens global health, food security, and development; however, the evolutionary and molecular pathways that drive AMR remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to advance diagnostics and rapidly detect newly emerging resistance. In this report, we employed laboratory evolution of an environmental Escherichia coli strain (NIST 0056) under B-lactam antibiotic pressure (ampicillin and cephalexin) to specifically investigate the relationship between resistance genotype and motility phenotype. Within 10 passages, populations evolved varying levels of B-lactam resistance (including high-level resistance > 32 ug/mL) and showed consistent, dose-dependent reductions in swimming motility. Whole-population genome sequencing revealed large deletions in marR, SNPs in efflux pump gene acrB and fumarate reductase gene frdD, and mutations with evidence of amplification in the chromosomal class C B-lactamase gene ampC, collectively linking these efflux-mediated, B-lactam resistance mechanisms to loss of motility. Notably, motility reductions were more pronounced in individual clones than in the mixed populations (p < 0.005, Mann-Whitney; two-tailed test). Following removal of antibiotic pressure, motility was restored and AMR-associated mutations decreased in frequency, suggesting fitness costs associated with resistance. In aggregate, our results demonstrate that reduced swimming motility accompanies specific efflux-driven, B-lactam resistance mechanisms. Further work will investigate if the behavior is generalizable across flagellated Enterobacteriaceae. Because these rapid changes are amenable to high-throughput measurement, swimming motility may offer a tractable physiological metric for AMR detection in environmental surveillance.

title: 41% of Gram-negative bacteria encode a Type Six Secretion System
content: The type six secretion system (T6SS) is a highly studied, versatile bacterial nanoweapon that is important in bacterial pathogenesis and evolution. Despite extensive study, its prevalence remains poorly quantified. Analyzing 35,467 representative genomes, we find that approximately 41% of genomes in the average well-sampled Gram-negative genus (more than 30 sampled genomes) encode a T6SS. Further, we show that the distribution of the T6SS is patchy at all taxonomic levels. The uneven distribution we found is consistent with context-dependent selection, repeated evolutionary loss, or greater evolutionary lability. Our dataset provides a foundation for studying the drivers of T6SS distribution, and our pipeline enables similar surveys of other secretion systems, gene clusters, and multi-protein complexes across bacteria.

title: Cell cycle progression and stalked cell morphogenesis in Caulobacter crescentus are regulated independently by the flagellum
content: Bacteria colonize surfaces and form biofilms to survive in stressful environmental conditions. Many bacteria use an appendage called the flagellum to sense surface contact, and responding to these mechanical cues triggers rapid physiological changes to promote downstream attachment. Bacteria are known to secrete adhesins and alter their motility behavior to facilitate surface colonization, but these changes alone are insufficient to explain the breadth of adaptations observed in surface-attached cells. Disrupting flagellar assembly in the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus constitutively activates the surface sensing pathway, and this gain-of-function phenotype was previously used to identify a suite of flagellar signaling suppressor (fss) genes that promotes surface adhesion downstream of the flagellum. We show herein that a subset of fss genes also regulates the C. crescentus developmental program. Live-cell microscopy analysis of fss mutants identified independent sub-pathways that target stalked cell morphogenesis and cell cycle progression. We identify the predicted chemotaxis genes fssD and fssE as novel regulators of stalked cell morphogenesis and show that these genes act to stimulate the diguanylate cyclase PleD in flagellar assembly mutants. A separate pathway that includes the stator protein MotB and the recently characterized dNTPase FssC regulates entry into S phase downstream of the flagellum. We show that motB regulates cell cycle progression specifically in response to surface cues, and that stator-dependent cell cycle control occurs independently of c-di-GMP and CtrA. This work clarifies the downstream targets of the surface sensing network and establishes a comprehensive model for how surface sensing influences the C. crescentus developmental program.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Translatomic Profiling Reveals Noncanonical RNA Junctions and Hidden Coding Potential in Porcine Epidemic Diarrhea Virus
content: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Although coronavirus discontinuous transcription is well characterized, the classical model cannot fully explain the diversity of viral RNA junctions, while conventional genome annotations may underestimate viral protein-coding capacity. To address these gaps, we integrated time-resolved RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), cycloheximide (CHX)- and harringtonine (HAR)-treated ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), comparative genomics, and peptide mass spectrometry to investigate PEDV RNA expression and hidden coding potential. RNA-seq revealed that, at 3 hours post-infection (hpi), the 3 genomic region exhibited strong relative coverage enrichment, whereas the relative contribution of the 5 replicase-coding region increased rapidly between 3 and 5 hpi, suggesting a possible transition from sgRNA-dominated RNA accumulation toward enhanced genomic RNA replication. Genome-wide junction analysis identified 43,635 distinct noncanonical RNA junctions, although canonical sgRNA junctions accounted for 95.5% of all junction-supporting reads. Several abundant noncanonical sgRNAs were predicted to generate novel coding products, including N-x4, N-x2, M-x3, and M-x2, short peptides encoded within the 3 untranslated region (UTR), and two distinct N-terminally truncated S proteins, thereby expanding the potential coding repertoire of PEDV. Genome-wide reading-frame analysis uncovered a pronounced asymmetry in hidden coding potential, identifying 68 overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) longer than 40 amino acids in the +1 reading frame, compared with only three in the +2 frame. Ribo-seq further revealed a progressive redistribution of viral ribosome occupancy toward structural protein-coding regions during the later stages of infection. By integrating HAR-associated translation initiation-site enrichment with CHX-based ORF-level translation analysis, we identified several noncanonical ORFs with strong translation-associated evidence, including N-x1, N-x2, S-x1, and ORF1b-x13. Moreover, peptide mass spectrometry detected a characteristic peptide corresponding to N-x1 in infected samples, providing independent proteomic evidence for the expression of this previously unannotated viral protein. Together, these findings uncover extensive noncanonical RNA synthesis and hidden protein-coding capacity in PEDV, establishing a foundation for understanding novel viral gene expression strategies and their potential evolutionary and pathogenic significance.

title: Diverse bacteria exhibit superadditive growth on mixed classes of carbon sources
content: Heterotrophic bacteria in nature encounter complex mixtures of functionally-distinct carbon sources, yet whether such diversity enhances growth yield across diverse taxa remains unknown. We grew dozens of strains from four phyla on defined mixtures representing five classes of carbon sources. Remarkably, many but not all strains exhibited superadditive growth on a dilute mixture of all 64 compounds--that is, yield exceeding the weighted sum of yields on more concentrated subsets of functionally-similar compounds. Using exometabolomics, pooled genetic screens, and proteomics, we find that superadditive growth is associated with enhanced carbon consumption in the mixed-class medium, combined with reduced dependence on amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis. Moreover, superadditive growth was predictable from genomes within the tested strain panel and correlated with genomically encoded sugar-over-acid preference. These findings reveal a previously underrecognized axis of physiological variation among heterotrophs and open the door to understanding the biochemical and evolutionary basis of this divergence.

title: Thienothiazolocarboxamides: rapidly cidal agents causing catastrophic thiol collapse in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
content: Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

title: The role of Plasmodium falciparum acyl-coenzyme A synthetase 10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis
content: During the asexual blood stage, malaria parasites synthesize large quantities of lipids to support their rapid proliferation. Exogenous fatty acids obtained from host plasma are activated for lipid synthesis by parasite acyl-coenzyme A synthetases (ACSs). Of the twelve Plasmodium falciparum ACS homologs, ACS10 has emerged as a key blood-stage enzyme. Here, we sought to define the role of ACS10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis during asexual development. To accomplish this, we have employed fatty acid alkyne probes of parasite lipid synthesis together with selective depletion of ACS10 in a conditional knockdown parasite line. This approach revealed that ACS10 is required for efficient incorporation of 16- to 20-carbon unsaturated fatty acid alkynes and a 20-carbon, saturated fatty acid alkyne into the major parasite phospholipids and neutral lipids. In contrast, shorter saturated fatty acid alkynes were either unaffected by ACS10 depletion or were hyper-incorporated into parasite lipids. ACS10 knockdown elicited a profound deformation of the food vacuole, which was likely caused by an imbalance of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids in parasite lipids. To promote the discovery and characterization of ACS inhibitors, we have established a fatty acid alkyne-based approach for identifying compounds that target ACS10 as their primary mode of action.

title: SPARK: Systematic Profiling of Antibiotic-Phage Response Kinetics
content: Phage therapy is, in practice, combination therapy: phage are almost always added to an ongoing antibiotic regimen, yet the combination is rarely designed to have a specific interaction pattern. Interactions can be antagonistic, additive or synergistic and cannot be inferred from either agent alone. Here we introduce SPARK, a method which quantifies phage antibiotic interaction from growth curves as the integrated deviation of observed growth from the growth expected under Bliss independence. We profiled 42 combinations spanning the ESKAPE pathogens and Escherichia coli with twelve antibiotics. We show that i) synergy and antagonism are resolvable within a single high-throughput assay, with the interaction determined by the phage antibiotic bacteria pairing; ii) 21 clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates differ among themselves as widely as the seven species do; and, iii) interactions change between a few hours and two days, several reversing direction. Overall, SPARK needs only a plate reader and the analysis is performed with a specific openly available web tool.

title: MmuPV1 and HPV E6 Elevate Nuclear Accumulation of IKK? to Impair NF-κB Signaling to Promote Persistent Infection
content: The mouse papillomavirus (MmuPV1) E6 oncoprotein is essential for persistent infection and cancer development. Previous studies identified amino acid R130 of MmuPV1 E6 as critical for its interaction with the tumor suppressor MAML1. Mutation of this residue (R130A) disrupts MAML1 binding and prevents disease development in mice. In this study, we demonstrate that MmuPV1 E6 also disrupts NF-{kappa}B signaling through interactions with proteins in the I{kappa}B kinase (IKK) complex. Specifically, the MmuPV1 E6R130A mutant is defective in binding IKK complex proteins and fails to impair NF-{kappa}B signaling in mouse keratinocytes, suggesting that these interactions are necessary for E6-mediated disruption of this pathway. Furthermore, MmuPV1 E6 expression is associated with increased nuclear localization of IKK?, whereas cells expressing the E6R130A mutant exhibit no such increase. These findings suggest that E6-mediated nuclear localization of IKK? depends on its interaction with IKK complex proteins. Importantly, we demonstrate that the human papillomavirus HPV16 E6 oncoprotein similarly impairs NF-{kappa}B signaling and increases nuclear IKK? localization in human keratinocytes, suggesting a shared mechanism between mouse and human papillomaviruses. Additionally, analysis of previously published RNA sequencing data reveals that MmuPV1 E6 induces several transcriptional changes associated with increased nuclear IKK?. Together, these findings demonstrate that both MmuPV1 and HPV16 E6 disrupt NF-{kappa}B signaling in association with increased nuclear IKK? localization. This study provides the first evidence of an E6 oncoprotein interacting with and changing subcellular localization of IKK? to disrupt cellular homeostasis.

title: Seasonal H1N1 influenza A virus preferentially infects a pre-existing ciliogenesis-primed secretory cell state
content: Influenza A viruses (IAV) infect secretory and ciliated cells of the human airway epithelium , but whether all cells within one cell type are equally susceptible to infection remains unresolved. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of primary human bronchial epithelial cultures from three donors identified preferential infection of a transcriptionally distinct subpopulation of secretory cells by seasonal H1N1 IAV A/Hawaii/70/2019 . Genes upregulated in this subpopulation showed enrichment for cilium-related gene ontology terms. In an ex post facto approach, this enrichment persisted after excluding genes differentially expressed between infected and mock-treated samples, including those identified in secretory cell-specific comparisons. Single-cell analysis further revealed no significant increase in ciliogenesis scores in infected secretory cells compared to mock infected cells at 6 hours post-infection , arguing against infection-induced activation of the canonical ciliogenesis programme during the initial viral replication cycle . Collectively, these results support preferential infection of ciliogenesis-primed secretory cells and refine IAV tropism beyond cell type to encompass epithelial differentiation state.

title: Structural and functional examination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae TfpC reveals a dynamic two-domain architecture required for type IV pilus function
content: The Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) Type IV pilus (T4p) is a critical apparatus for colonization and virulence. This molecular machine resides at the host-pathogen interface and mediates adherence to host cells, twitching motility, natural transformation, and resistance to oxidative agents. Previously, we identified a DUF4124 family, T4p component, TfpC. TfpC is required for full T4p elaboration, and deleting the tfpC gene reduced natural transformation competence and resulted in an under-piliated colony morphology. Our earlier models suggested TfpC is composed of an N-terminal transmembrane helix and a proline-rich disordered region followed by a C-terminal coiled-coil. Here, we used targeted structural and genetic approaches to define TfpC's molecular structure. Our new data show that TfpC's N-terminal domain forms a novel, dynamic three-stranded {beta}-sheet structure. These data indicate that the flexible disordered region acts as a linker between the N- and C-terminal domains. Functionally, we illustrate TfpC requires an acidic face within the C-terminal coiled-coil domain to mediate pilus biogenesis and function. This study characterizes a unique protein fold and family and defines the contributions of TfpC's domains to its function.

title: Polyphosphate metabolism genes are associated with hydroxyapatite biomineralization capacity in a novel hydrogenotrophic methanogen Methanobacterium AMB_03
content: Methanogenic archaea play crucial roles in sedimentary phosphorus cycling, but their capacity for phosphate biomineralization remains poorly understood. Here we demonstrate that Methanobacterium AMB_03, isolated from a serpentinizing environment, mediates extracellular precipitation of carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite (HAp) under phosphate-enriched conditions. Comparative genomic analysis of AMB_03 versus non-mineralizing strains (Methanobacterium oryzae, Methanoculleus bourgensis MAB1) shows that AMB_03 encodes polyphosphate kinase 1 (ppk1), enabling polyphosphate synthesis from ATP. In contrast, M. oryzae and MAB1 completely lack ppk1, preventing polyphosphate accumulation. Phylogenomic analysis of 320 Methanobacteriota genomes further shows that complete polyP cycling capacity is present in only ~25% of representatives, placing AMB_03 among a minority of methanogens with this capability. Experimental cultivation across phosphate gradients (0-6 mM) showed HAp early-onset precipitation was preferential at [≥]3 mM. Precipitation was eventually observed at all phosphate concentrations (except P0) by 49 weeks and was associated with extracellular polymeric substance production and localized pH increases of up to 8.08. Raman spectroscopy confirmed carbonate-substituted HAp, with characteristic peaks at 960.5 cm-1 (PO43-) and 1070-1072 cm-1 (CO32-). These findings identify a strong genomic association between polyphosphate metabolism genes and biomineralization capacity, suggesting that methanogens with complete polyP cycling systems may create localized phosphate-rich environments that promote authigenic mineral formation in sedimentary systems.

title: Environmental Frass Remodels the Larval Gut Microbiome to Enable Black Soldier Fly (Hermetia illucens) Bioconversion of Livestock Manure
content: Black Soldier Fly larvae (BSFL) consume nearly any organic material and show promise for the remediation of agricultural waste, including livestock manure. BSFL feeding generates frass, a mixture of unconsumed substrate, larval feces, and microorganisms. We identified a wild population of BSFL (Yuba strain) thriving on rabbit manure, a challenging substrate due to its high lignocellulose content. We investigated if frass extract from this source was necessary and sufficient to support bioconversion of manure and if such effects are altered by captive husbandry. Larvae supplemented with domestic frass failed to grow on rabbit manure but grew well when supplemented with wild-sourced frass. Microbiome analysis revealed that wild-sourced frass contributes a cohort of lignocellulose-degrading microorganisms to the BSFL gut, particularly Rummeliibacillus bacteria and Scedosporium fungi. These growth-promoting effects extended to cattle manure. Following initial seeding with wild-sourced frass, lab-cultured frass ultimately failed to support growth on rabbit manure and the gut microbiome shifted toward bacteria commonly found in domestic BSFL. This study reveals that frass extract derived from environmental sources can improve the bioconversion ability of BSFL and that beneficial microbes are lost during captive-rearing.

title: Integrating Microbial Ecology and Sustainability: Linking Agricultural Waste Gas Streams to Microbial Community Shifts in a Photobioreactor
content: Photobioreactors (PBRs) coupled to animal housing offer potential for mitigating gaseous emissions such as CO2 and NH3 while simultaneously producing biomass. Here, we present a time-resolved characterization of microbial community dynamics, with a focus on the genetic potential for carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Using a cone-shaped, helical PBR cultivating Arthrospira platensis (Spirulina) and supplied with exhaust air from a chicken house, we characterized microbial communities over continuous exhaust-air exposure and periodic biomass harvesting. Microbiome and gene-centric profiling revealed temporal variation in community composition and in the representation of genes associated with carbon and nitrogen metabolism. Cycle-based dissolved inorganic nitrogen balances showed that the decrease in dissolved inorganic nitrogen was only partially recovered in harvested biomass, while ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms were associated with structured, low-light niches. These observations indicate ammonia-oxidizing potential but do not establish a quantitatively relevant nitrification flux. Structured carrier matrices provided attached-growth niches harboring microbial populations underrepresented in the circulating suspension, while pre-colonized carriers facilitated biomass development during re-inoculation. Overall, our results show that coupling PBRs to agricultural exhaust streams can support biomass production while sustaining spatially structured microbial communities with taxonomic and functional potential. These findings may inform their further development for emission mitigation and circular biomass production.

title: Engineered DNA materials shape microbial physiology and ecological selection
content: Extracellular DNA (eDNA) is both a structural component of microbial biofilms and a potential reservoir of genetic information, yet its role as an ecological material remains largely unexplored. Here we establish engineered extracellular materials as determinants of microbial physiology and community assembly across increasing biological complexity. A three-dimensional DNA hydrogel altered bacterial stress-associated responses, elicited species-dependent phenotypes and transcriptional changes in a defined consortium, and shaped community succession in wastewater-derived microbiomes. Distinct responses to surface-bound oligonucleotides reveal that DNA presentation matters beyond its mere presence. Strikingly, metagenomic sequencing identified rare, hydrogel-specific candidate junctions linking material-derived DNA to microbial genomic sequences, suggesting a previously unexplored interface between extracellular DNA materials and microbial genetic information. These findings reveal a dual role for engineered DNA: its material organization shapes microbial physiology and ecological selection, while its encoded sequences may engage with microbial genomic processes.

title: Polyphyletic origins and lineage-specific expansion of chemosensory systems in phylum Actinomycetota
content: Phylum Actinomycetota (syn. Actinobacteriota or Actinobacteria), one of the largest well-studied bacterial phyla, is renowned for complex morphology, non-motility, ecological versatility, and secondary metabolite production. Chemosensory systems (CSS) are among the most sophisticated prokaryotic signal transduction architectures, yet their evolutionary distribution in this phylum remains poorly understood. Here, a comparative genomic analysis of 693 high-quality genomes spanning the phylum resolves the diversity, distribution, and evolutionary trajectories of CSS. Despite extensive genomic complexity and ecological versatility, only 6.9% of genomes encode complete CSS clusters, confined to a subset of lineages within a few classes, indicating lineage-specific retention or loss. In contrast, two-component systems (TCS) are ubiquitously abundant, with hybrid kinases enriched in CSS-deficient classes, suggesting functional compensation for the absence of dedicated chemosensory pathways. Basal lineages retain simplified CSS (F1 or F5), whereas Actinomycetes show lineage-specific expansion into multiple classes (F5, F8, F9, and ACF), often co-occurring, indicative of enhanced sensory complexity. The phylogeny of CheA homologs shows a polyphyletic distribution, supporting a mosaic evolutionary history shaped by multiple independent acquisitions, diversification, and gene loss. Collectively, our findings show that, unlike motile bacteria, members of Actinomycetota rely predominantly on TCS-driven regulatory networks, with CSS retained only in select lineages where ecological demands require enhanced environmental sensing. This work provides a phylum-wide evolutionary framework for the emergence, diversification, and functional specialization of CSS in non-motile bacteria.

title: The ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) of Iceland
content: The native terrestrial biota of Iceland required long oceanic journeys to colonize the island. Human colonization of Iceland, however, has allowed many less vagile species, such as ants, to reach the island. We compiled published, unpublished, and new records of ants from Iceland and evaluated the probable origin and current status of each species. We analyzed 565 records compiled by the Icelandic Institute of Natural History (1974-2020) and 84 new records (2019-2023) representing 25 species. Only five species were found living outdoors: Hypoponera ergatandria (507x indoors and 9x outdoors, mostly in geothermal areas), Lasius niger (24x indoors and 12x outdoors away from heated buildings), Hypoponera eduardi (5x only in geothermal areas), Lasius platythorax (1x near a small greenhouse and 1x in imported plant material), and Myrmica rubra (1x in an urban garden). Three ant species were exclusively found inhabiting heated buildings: Monomorium pharaonis (41x), Tapinoma melanocephalum (10x), and Monomorium nr. pharaonis (3x). Records of the remaining 17 species all appear to be based on temporary infestations, found on recently imported plant material. Previous records from Iceland of Hypoponera punctatissima appear to be based on misidentifications. Although it is possible that some ants were present before human arrival, all 25 ant species may have arrived accompanying humans. It remains to be seen whether any of these ant species are having or will have a significant impact on the native Icelandic biota. The arrival of Myrmica rubra in Iceland is particularly worrisome, given the impact this species is having in other high latitude areas it has invaded.

title: Natural regeneration in tree islands drives long-term recovery of native forest-associated woody species in oil palm landscapes
content: 1. Large-scale conversion of tropical rainforests to oil palm plantations is a major driver of biodiversity loss in Southeast Asia, particularly threatening native forest-associated plant species and their associated biota. Integrating tree islands within monocultural oil palm landscapes has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate biodiversity loss. However, their effectiveness in sustaining natural regeneration and long-term recovery of native forest-associated plant species remains unclear. 2. We analyzed temporal trajectories of diversity, abundance, and composition of naturally recruiting woody species in tree islands embedded in a monoculture-dominated landscape. We used a large-scale biodiversity enrichment experiment with 52 tree islands, varying in area (25 - 1600 m2) and planted tree diversity (0, 1, 2, 3, or 6 species), established in a conventional oil palm plantation in Sumatra, Indonesia, in 2013. 3. Across four censuses conducted between 2 and 8 years after the onset of natural regeneration, we found 82 species of recruiting woody plants (trees and shrubs) belonging to 64 genera and 34 families. At the landscape (gamma) scale, species richness and abundance increased by ~42% and ~69%, respectively, from 2018 to 2024, with shifts in community evenness and continued species arrival. After 8 years, neither richness nor abundance saturated, indicating continued accumulation of recruiting plant species. 4. Tree islands promoted natural regeneration of native diversity, with 90% of species and individuals being native. Native forest-associated species (N = 35) increased steadily at the landscape scale, while localized dominance of alien species did not indicate arrested succession. 5. At the local (alpha) scale, larger island area exerted a sustained positive effect on recruiting diversity. Higher initial planted tree diversity promoted native recruitment, particularly of forest-associated species, at earlier stages, an effect that diminished over time. 6. Synthesis and applications. Tree islands promote natural regeneration and accelerate recovery of native forest-associated diversity over extended periods, providing an effective strategy to enhance forest-associated biodiversity within oil palm landscapes. Preserving the last remaining lowland rainforests, irreplaceable reservoirs of native forest-associated species, remains essential to support continued recruitment into tree islands that can create stepping-stone habitats and a more wildlife-friendly agricultural matrix.

title: Assembly of host-specific bacterial and fungal communities from soil by diverse subaerial green algae
content: Green algae recruit microbes from their environment to the phycosphere, a region closely surrounding algal cells which is analogous to the rhizosphere of land plants. Recent work showed that subaerial green algae can recruit and assemble their phycosphere microbiota from soil-derived bacteria. However, how widespread this ability is among diverse green algae, whether host identity shapes community composition, and whether soil-borne fungi can be recruited to the phycosphere remained unclear. Here, we show that subaerial green algae spanning Chlorophyta and Streptophyta assemble distinct phycosphere communities from soil-derived bacteria and fungi, with host identity as the primary driver of phycosphere composition, both in natural soil and in a liquid mesocosm. In soil, bacterial communities were strongly reshaped by algal hosts, whereas the fungal communities responded more weakly and less consistently. In liquid system, bacterial community composition was correlated with host phylogeny. Phycosphere communities included taxa known to associate with land plants in the rhizosphere, supporting the finding that some microbial taxa associate with a wide range of photosynthetic hosts. Our findings demonstrate that the green algae capacity to assemble distinct phycosphere communities possibly predates the divergence of Chlorophyta and Streptophyta. The stronger effect of host identity on bacterial than fungal community mirrors patterns observed in land plant microbiota, suggesting that principles of host-microbe interactions are conserved across evolutionarily distant photosynthetic hosts.

title: A tabular foundation model rivals established species distribution models from presence-only records
content: Predicting where something occurs from records of where it has been observed, without reliable records of absence, is a common problem in science. Species distribution models (SDMs) such as MaxEnt address it in fields from biological conservation and climate-change assessment to the mapping of disease vectors and archaeological sites, but must be tuned for each dataset. Tabular foundation models, pre-trained on synthetic prediction tasks, predict new datasets without per-dataset training. Only one study has tested them as SDMs, and it fine-tuned on survey data from the evaluated regions. We evaluated tabular foundation models on the standard SDM benchmark (225 species in six regions, with independent presence-absence surveys), under the protocol used to compare 21 methods, and on 120 virtual species with known distributions. Without tuning, a tabular foundation model, TabPFN 3.5, equalled the best published approach, a five-model ensemble (mean AUC 0.732). Fine-tuned on presence-background tasks from other regions, it became the best single model on the benchmark (0.736), outperformed MaxEnt (0.728) and boosted regression trees after correction for multiple comparisons, and was better calibrated than MaxEnt, although six regions were too few to establish the advantage for new regions. Fine-tuning on presence-absence surveys of other species helped only when they came from the evaluated regions. On virtual species, it recovered simple additive relationships less well than regression-based methods but complex ones at least as well when records were unbiased, and was worse with environmentally biased records. Tabular foundation models are competitive SDMs without per-dataset tuning, but they are sensitive to environmentally biased records.

title: Population dynamics in extreme environments: shared histories of strong selection lead to predictable patterns across separate high-elevation populations of small mammals
content: Many frameworks exist to identify species that are vulnerable to environmental change, but we still generally lack the ability to anticipate species' responses when changes occur. Exploring patterns of trait evolution along environmental gradients could help this process: conditions become more predictable and less variable at the ends of gradients, with past studies hypothesizing that consistently harsh environments will result in predictable evolutionary patterns. To test this hypothesis, we characterized genetic and phenotypic variation, as well as selection on this variation, in deer mice (Peromyscus maniculatus) along two transects spanning from 2120-4200m in the Colorado Rocky Mountains, U.S.A. We found that both genetic and phenotypic variation declined with elevation, that high elevation populations had higher rates of survival, and that fewer traits influenced survival at high elevations. These results suggest extreme environments may lead to predictable consequences for populations and provide a basis for forecasting population vulnerability to environmental change.

title: Slowed aquatic invasion coincides with intensified research and prevention in Minnesota, USA
content: Prevention is often the most cost-effective expenditure of limited environmental management resources. While demonstrating that harms occur without prevention is relatively straightforward, showing harms have lessened due to prevention--proving its effectiveness--is not, in part because it requires counterfactual data (i.e., quantification of harms that did not occur and then attributing these to prevention). Here, we attempt to measure aquatic invasive species (AIS) prevention effectiveness in Minnesota, USA, where AIS, their management, and research have increased since the 1980s. We showed the rate of new aquatic invasions slowed alongside intensified prevention investment starting around 2015. Further, mechanistic simulations grounded in real boater movement and boat inspection effectiveness data suggested prevention may have reduced new invasions of two high-priority AIS by 20-53% over a ten-year span. We argue our evidence strongly supports long-term statewide prevention, monitoring, and research.

title: Phenotypic variation in divergent mitochondrial haplotypes in migratory three-spined stickleback
content: Mitochondria are essential components in life-sustaining organismal processes. The mitochondrial genome can be influenced by selection, and divergent mitochondrial haplotypes have substantial potential to affect interspecies variation in life-history and physiology, yet little is known about whole organism phenotypic changes that might accompany mitochondrial genomic divergence. Three-spined stickleback on the Scottish island of North Uist provide a model to study this as their populations exhibit a well-mixed nuclear genome, yet two highly diverged mitochondrial haplotypes ( trans-Atlantic and  European). Three-spined stickleback were sampled from six lochs to investigate associations between mitochondrial haplotype and phenotypic traits including organ size, body size, and ovule volume/clutch size, as well as citrate synthase enzyme activity. Results showed that mitochondrial haplotype has an influence on male gonadosomatic index (GSI) and potentially citrate synthase (CS) enzyme activity. Differences in male GSI may be explained by the timing of male spermatogenesis or potentially a need for larger testes in European haplotype fish. While no other phenotypic trait showed differences between mitochondrial haplotypes, there were many differences between sexes and populations e.g. in body size and organ/muscle size.

title: Disease dynamics during ecosystem restoration and faunal reassembly
content: Biodiversity recovery is increasingly promoted as a strategy for restoring ecosystem services, including the regulation of infectious diseases. However, it remains unclear how the potential for pathogen transmission interacts with the timing of biodiversity recovery and the life history of the recovering species to shape the disease dynamics during restoration. Here, we developed a stochastic multi-host metacommunity epidemic model to investigate how the timing of the establishment of slow life history species, pathogen transmissibility, and host-community succession jointly influence disease outcomes in recovering ecosystems. Pathogen transmissibility (R_0) was the dominant predictor of epidemic intensity, whereas the delayed timing of establishment of slow life history species during restoration emerged as a major ecological determinant of pathogen persistence. Delayed establishment of slow life-history hosts consistently increased disease prevalence and persistence by prolonging the dominance of highly competent fast life-history hosts. Generalized additive models revealed a strong interaction between delayed timing of slow life-history species establishment and pathogen transmissibility, explaining more than 90% of the variation in pathogen persistence. The influence of timing of establishment of slow life history species was weak for pathogens with low transmission potential but increased markedly as R_0 increased. Sensitivity analyses further showed that, once pathogen transmissibility was controlled, timing of establishment became the strongest predictor of persistence, whereas among-host spillover transmission primarily influenced the speed of epidemic spread. In contrast, maximum species richness had comparatively little influence on disease outcomes, indicating that the functional composition and assembly timing of recovering communities may be more important than richness alone for predicting disease dynamics. Together, these results demonstrate that disease regulation during ecosystem restoration depends not only on pathogen transmissibility, but also on the life history traits and the timing of establishment of species within recovering communities. Our findings identify life history traits and the timing of when functional communities are restored as a key ecological lever influencing long-term pathogen maintenance in restored ecosystems.

title: Two decades of EU pesticide substitution have not reduced impacts on stream invertebrates
content: Chemical regulation assumes that withdrawing hazardous substances and replacing them with alternatives reduces environmental harm. We tested this premise within the EU pesticide regulatory framework using a 23-year record of event-driven pesticide exposure and stream-invertebrate communities from 152 German agricultural streams sampled between 1998 and 2021. Neither pesticide toxic pressure nor pesticide-related invertebrate impairment showed a detectable decline over time, and an improvement equivalent to one ecological status class can be excluded. Dominant toxicity drivers shifted from organophosphates to neonicotinoids and subsequently to pyrethroids, yet the relationship between toxic pressure and community effects remained consistent despite their distinct modes of action. Sustained toxic pressure reflected three mechanisms: successive chemical substitution, prolonged approval periods, and continued exposure to substances no longer authorised as plant protection products. Substitution thus changed which chemicals harm streams, not how much. Measured field outcomes must become the benchmark of pesticide regulation.

title: Gregariousness can promote invasion success of pest insects while higher environmental heterogeneity decreases it
content: Climate change and environmental homogenization are expected to facilitate the expansion of many forest pest insect species and increase the vulnerability of forest ecosystems to insect outbreaks. At present, we lack empirical data on how the antipredator defence traits of pest insects interact with the local environmental conditions and shape outbreak risk. Here we study this and ask 1) how the antipredator defence strategy of pest insects shapes survival under naturally varying predator community, and 2) how is predation risk shaped by the diversity and structure of forests? We tested these questions by conducting a field predation experiment with artificial prey system (prey items made from edible dough) where we manipulated the gregariousness, unpalatability and defensive colouration of prey and tested their effects on prey survival. Additionally, we measured environmental variables and invertebrate predator community structure along the prey transects to analyse how they shape overall predation risk. Our results show that the predation risk was always lowest for gregarious prey irrespective of other defence strategies. Furthermore, our results indicate that predation pressure was lower in more homogenously structured forest areas or areas with a weak quality deadwood continuum in comparison to locations with more natural state forests and good quality deadwood continuum. Altogether, our results suggest that gregariousness can facilitate pest insects to form outbreaks by increasing their survival against generalist predators. However, by maintaining higher heterogeneity in forests, it is possible to ensure higher predation pressure to regulate their population growth.

title: Tree cavities as attractors: an experimental test of the effects of woodpecker legacy on local bird activity and species richness
content: Tree cavities, whether excavated by birds or formed through wood decay, are key structural features of forest ecosystems. They are critical resources for secondary cavity users and influence breeding bird assemblages by affecting the occurrence and abundance of certain species. However, the effect of an individual cavity on fine-scale bird activity, independently of the surrounding habitat context, remains poorly understood. Here, we experimentally tested the effect of cavity presence on bird activity in a coniferous forest in southern Poland. We installed pairs of standardized, debarked snags, each consisting of one snag with an artificial entrance resembling a woodpecker-excavated cavity and one control snag without a cavity entrance. Bird presence and activity were monitored using camera traps and vegetation structure was quantified around each snag. The presence of a cavity entrance had a positive effect on visitation rates and species richness. Snags with cavity entrances received 114% more bird visits than control snags (4.5 [95% CI: 3.1-6.5] vs 2.1 [1.4-3.2]) and were visited by 48% more species (2.0 [1.5-2.6] vs 1.3 [0.9-1.9]). In addition, greater canopy closure around snags was associated with higher visitation rates and species richness. Our study demonstrates that a single cavity can act as a fine-scale attractor for forest birds. These findings highlight the role of cavities and cavity-bearing trees in shaping spatially heterogeneous patterns of fine-scale habitat use by birds.
